title: 道德經 第三十章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 30, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 67. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 30 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 儉武 (Sparing of Arms). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
以道佐人主者，
不以兵強天下。

morph.gloss: to assist, to serve as second to
the lord of men — the standing term for a sovereign
the one who — closes and nominalises everything before it
weapons; troops, arms — the whole business of war
to be strong, to play the strong man (qiáng; read qiǎng it would be 'to coerce')

sentences.l:
One who by the Way assists the lord of men
does not by arms play strong among all-under-heaven.
sentences.i: He who serves a ruler by the Way does not use arms to make himself the strong man among all under heaven.
sentences.n: 者 gathers up the whole clause before it and makes a noun of it — 'the one who does all that'. The chapter's one contested word is 強. Read qiǎng it is transitive, 'to coerce all under heaven'; read qiáng it is stative, 'to be the strong man among all under heaven'. Wang Bi paraphrases the line with 於 inserted — 強於天下, strong *in* all under heaven — which shows he took it the second way, and under our rule the commentary decides. The other reading is a real one, and 強 comes back twice more before the chapter closes.

morph.gloss: that, such — pointing back to the use of arms
business, the affair, the thing done
is apt to, is given to (hào 'to be fond of'; hǎo would be the adjective 'good')
to come back, to return upon

sentences.l: That business is apt to come back.
sentences.i: That kind of business has a way of coming back round.
sentences.n: Four characters, and the whole of the chapter's argument. 好 does not mean 'good' here: with a verb after it, it says that a thing tends to do something, is fond of doing it — the affair *likes* coming back. 還 is simply 'to come back', and Wang Bi keeps it so: he expands it as 還反, turning back and reverting, setting the man who starts things, bent on making a name and generating business, against the man of the Way, who is bent on reverting to acting without forcing. The English keeps 還 plain, so the coming-back can be read as Wang Bi reads it and also as the next lines illustrate it — brambles and famine, the deed returning on the doer.

sentences.t:
師之所處，
荊棘生焉。
大軍之後，
必有凶年。

morph.gloss: an army, a host on campaign — a full army in the field
of — genitive here, not the object pronoun
that which, the place where — 所 before a verb makes a noun of it
to settle, to encamp, to take one's place (chǔ; as a noun, chù, 'a place')
thorn and bramble — the scrub that takes a field when no one works it
there, in that place — a fused word, 於 'in' + 之 'it'
an army, a body of troops
a year of dearth — the standing term for a failed harvest, not merely an unlucky year
a year; a harvest, the crop of a year

sentences.l:
Where an army has settled,
thorn and bramble spring up there.
In the wake of a great army,
there is bound to be a year of dearth.
sentences.n: 所 is one of the small words that does the most work: put before a verb it makes a noun of it — 所處 'the where-it-settles', the place occupied. 焉 then closes the line by fusing the preposition and its pronoun into one syllable, 於 'in' plus 之 'it': 'grows there'. The reason for the famine is agricultural and not mystical — the men who would have sown are away, so scrub takes the fields and there is no crop. The two couplets close on 焉 and 年, which do chime in Mandarin (yān / nián); in Old Chinese they belonged to two neighbouring rhyme groups rather than one, so this is a half-rhyme at best — treat it as a chime, not as proof of a pattern.

sentences.t:
善有果而已，
不敢以取強。

morph.gloss: the good one, one who is good at it — the adjective standing as a noun
to have, to come away with
the outcome, the thing brought off — 果 is a fruit, hence what an action bears
that is all, and no more (已 as the final particle again)
by that means, thereby — 以 with its object (the force of arms) left unsaid
mastery, the upper hand — the adjective 'strong' as a noun (qiáng)

sentences.l:
The good one has his outcome, and that is all;
he does not dare thereby to take mastery.
sentences.i: One who is good at it gets the thing done and no more; he does not presume to go on and seize mastery.
sentences.n: Wang Bi glosses 果 by 濟, to bring through, to see a thing safely over — the outcome here is the trouble relieved, not a victory won. 而已, 'and stop', is the ordinary classical way of saying 'and no further'; it will come back constantly. Notice 以 with nothing after it: an object that the passage has already made plain is simply left out. Wang Bi supplies it when he restates the line — 不以兵力取強於天下, 'does not by force of arms take mastery in all under heaven' — so what is dropped is the army, the means, not the outcome just named.

sentences.t:
果而勿矜，
果而勿伐，
果而勿驕。

morph.gloss: to bring it off, to get the outcome — the noun used as a verb
do not — the prohibitive negative, used to forbid rather than to deny
to plume oneself, to stand on one's own worth
to vaunt, to beat one's own drum (the character's first sense is to hew, to strike)
to be arrogant, to carry oneself high — first said of a spirited horse

sentences.i: Get it done, and take no pride in it; get it done, and make no boast of it; get it done, and give yourself no airs.
sentences.n: 勿 is not 不: it is the prohibitive, the negative that forbids rather than denies, and it normally swallows its object, so 勿矜 is 'do not plume yourself on it'. 果 was a noun in the line before — an outcome — and is a verb here, to bring the outcome about; nothing on the page marks the change, which is the ordinary condition of a Chinese word. Two of the three vices you have already met: 自伐 and 自矜, self-vaunting and self-esteem, are what chapter 24 pinned on the man who gets nothing done, and what chapter 22 said the sage does without. The third, 驕, came in chapter 9 — 富貴而驕, rich and honoured and swaggering with it.

sentences.t:
果而不得已，
果而勿強。

morph.gloss: and — here it joins the deed to the one condition on which it is allowed
to stop, to leave off — so 不得已 is 'cannot stop', there is no help for it
be strong, make might of it (qiáng)

sentences.l:
Bring it off, and only where there is no help for it;
bring it off, and do not make might of it.
sentences.i: Get it done, and only when there was no other course; get it done, and do not turn it into strength.
sentences.n: Here are the three characters chapter 29 used the other way. There 不得已 was 不得 'does not get' with the final particle 已; here it is the set idiom — literally 'cannot stop' — meaning that there was no alternative, which is this book's only permission to fight at all. Two identical writings, two different sentences, and only the sense of the passage to tell you which you have. Chapter 31 uses the idiom again of the same subject.

sentences.t:
物壯則老，
是謂不道，
不道早已。

morph.gloss: at full vigour, in its prime, grown mighty
is called, is what one calls
to go the Way, to act by it — 不 negates verbs, so 道 is a verb here
comes to an end — 已 as a full verb here, to stop, to be done

sentences.l:
A creature at full vigour then grows old:
this is called not-going-the-Way,
and not-going-the-Way comes early to its end.
sentences.i: A thing at its mightiest is already ageing: this is called not going by the Way, and what does not go by the Way is soon finished.
sentences.n: Two small lessons meet in this line. 不 negates verbs and adjectives, never nouns — a noun takes 非 — so 不道 cannot be 'not the Way' as a thing; 道 is being used as a verb, to go by the Way, and 不道 is the conduct that does not. And 已, which has closed a clause in this chapter as a mere particle, is here the full verb it started as: to stop, to have done. The thought is chapter 23's: a gusting wind does not last out the morning. 老 lǎo and 道 dào rhyme in Mandarin and belonged to the same Old Chinese rhyme group, so here the rhyme really has survived — worth reading aloud. These three clauses turn up again almost word for word in chapter 55, with 謂之 in place of 是謂.
